guides.title: A Harder Righteousness
guides.eyebrow: A six-session study on the Sermon on the Mount, and the kingdom it describes.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who have heard the Sermon on the Mount preached as a set of impossible ideals nobody is expected to keep, or as a handful of nice sayings stripped from the kingdom that gives them teeth. It is neither. It walks slowly through six movements across Matthew 5 through 7, on the Beatitudes and the upside-down kingdom they announce, on salt and light and the deeper law that reaches anger and lust before they reach the hand, on the love of enemies and the cost of refusing to retaliate, on treasure and money and the worry that follows a divided heart, on judging and asking and the narrow gate, and on the two houses and the storm that tells you which one you actually built. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than advice.

This is not a study that softens the Sermon into advice. Bell will not let it, and the leader must not either. Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote that when Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die, and he wrote it about this very sermon, against a church that had turned grace into something cheap and the demands of Jesus into something optional. The Sermon on the Mount is the most quoted and least obeyed teaching in human history, and the gap between the quoting and the obeying is where this study lives. It refuses two easy escapes at once, the one that says these are only ideals for a perfect world and excuses us from them, and the one that says these are rules we keep by trying harder and turns the gospel back into law. Most of all it implicates the writer and the leader. Bell does not stand on the mountain looking down. He has nursed an anger he called principle. He has loved his money and called it stewardship. He has built on sand and decorated the house so no one could tell. He preaches this sermon as a man it convicts. So will you.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: After Christendom
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on following Jesus faithfully in a world that no longer pretends to be Christian.
guides.blurb:
This study is for thoughtful Christians, for pastors who feel the ground shifting under their feet, and for small groups willing to look at the present honestly instead of mourning a past that was never as Christian as we remember it. It walks slowly through five movements drawn from James Bell's book After Christendom, on the end of cultural Christianity and why its passing may be a mercy, on the church learning again to live as exiles the way Jeremiah told the captives in Babylon to live, on witness offered without the protection of power, on becoming a creative minority rather than a defeated one, and on a hope that does not run on nostalgia. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than strategy.

This is not a study that tells the church to fight harder to win back a culture that has left. It will not do that, and the leader must not let it. The temptation in a moment like this is to reach for one of two false comforts. The first is panic, the conviction that the sky is falling and the answer is a louder, angrier defense of the territory we are losing. The second is denial, the pretense that nothing has changed and a little more effort will set it all back the way it was. Bell refuses both. Cultural Christianity is ending, and that is simply true. But the end of Christendom is not the end of the church, and it may be the beginning of something the church has not been in a long time, smaller, stranger, freer, more like the thing that turned the Roman world upside down before it had a single law on its side. Most of all the study implicates the writer and the leader. Bell does not stand outside this as a prophet announcing other people's failure. He pastored through the years when the pews thinned, watched his own assumptions about Christian America fall apart, and found that he had built more of his ministry on cultural Christianity than on Christ than he wanted to admit. He writes from inside the loss. So will you.
guides.audience: Thoughtful Christians, pastors, and small groups in a secular age

guides.title: Alone in a Crowded Church
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on loneliness, belonging, and the community Christ actually promised.
guides.blurb:
This study is for anyone who has stood in a full sanctuary, sung every word, shaken every hand at the door, and driven home knowing that not one person in that building could have told you what was wrong. It is for small groups, adult classes, and the church leaders who built the program and cannot understand why the people inside it are still so alone. It walks slowly through five movements drawn from James Bell's book Alone in a Crowded Church, on the difference between attendance and belonging, on the koinonia the first believers actually practiced in Acts, on the friendship the modern church has quietly let die, on the hospitality and the burden-bearing the New Testament commands of us toward one another, and on the long, unglamorous work of being known. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than a program.

This is not a study that scolds lonely people for not trying harder to plug in. It will not do that, and the leader must never let it. The hard truth this study refuses to soften is that the church itself often manufactures the very loneliness it laments. We built buildings you can hide in. We mistook a crowd for a body and attendance for love. We made the coffee hour a performance where everyone reports that they are fine. Bell does not stand outside this indictment. He has pastored a church of hundreds and felt unknown inside his own congregation. He has asked how are you and not waited for the answer. He has let a member drift out the back door and told himself they were busy. He writes from inside the loneliness, as one of the people who helped build the room where it grows. So will you.
guides.audience: Anyone who has felt alone in church, small groups, and church leaders

guides.title: Believe
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on what Christians actually believe, and why it is both reasonable and life-giving.
guides.blurb:
This study is for new believers taking their first honest steps, for seekers who are circling the faith with real questions, and for small groups willing to slow down and ask what the gospel even is before anyone is asked to sign on to it. It walks slowly through five movements drawn from James Bell's book Believe, on whether there is a God at all and what kind, on who Jesus claimed to be and why the claim cannot be sidestepped, on whether he actually rose from a tomb, on faith and doubt and the difference between certainty and trust, and on what it costs and what it gives to follow him. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than in winning an argument.

This is not a study that treats doubt as the enemy or seekers as projects to be closed. It will not do that, and the leader must never let it. Faith is not the absence of questions, and a faith that has never been tested is not strong, it is merely untested. Some objections to Christianity are bad and collapse under their own weight. Some are serious, honest, and have been asked by the church's best minds for two thousand years, and those deserve a real answer and not a slogan. The study holds both without flinching. Most of all it implicates the writer. Bell does not stand outside this. He came to faith out of atheism, which means he has sat on the other side of the table and meant his objections. He was raised without a father, which shapes how he hears the word Father applied to God. He still has mornings the doubt comes back. He writes from inside the questions, not from a safe distance above them. So will you.
guides.audience: New believers, seekers, small groups, and adult Sunday school

guides.title: Character Before Competence
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on leading the church without losing your soul.
guides.blurb:
This study is for pastors, elders, deacons, and the leadership teams who carry a church together, and it is for anyone who has felt the gap between the man the work demands and the man he actually is. It walks slowly through five movements drawn from James Bell's book Character Before Competence, on the qualifications God actually screens for, on the inner life and the exhaustion no one sees, on the idol of being needed and the burnout that grows from it, on who you put in the room and why no man is safe to lead alone, and on the three that fell most of the leaders we have lost and the final work of raising the one who comes after. It is built to be run by a busy leadership team with little preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than strategy.

This is not a study that lets the gifted off the hook because the numbers are good, and it is not a study that despises competence. A man who cannot teach should not be appointed to teach, and a treasurer who cannot read a balance sheet is a liability dressed as a volunteer. Skill is not nothing. The point is order. Character is the foundation and competence is the house, and a house with no foundation is not a bargain. It is a delay. The study holds both without flinching, and refuses to let the church keep reading God's two lists upside down. Most of all it implicates the leader and the writer. Bell does not stand outside this. He has run the search that let the gift do the screening character was supposed to do. He has handled the things of God all week and not eaten a bite. He has built a bottleneck with his own face on it and prayed to it daily without naming it. He writes from inside the same room the fallen fell in. So will you.
guides.audience: Pastors, elders, deacons, and leadership teams

guides.title: Christian Nationalism: An 8-Week Study
guides.eyebrow: A pastoral, even-handed five-session study that names what Christian nationalism is and is not, indicts every tribe, and keeps the cross over the flag.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who are tired of a phrase that has been thrown like a rock in two directions and want to know what it actually names. It walks slowly through five essays by James Bell, defining Christian nationalism without slandering the man whose grandfather landed at Normandy, and confronting the fusion of nation and faith without sneering at ordinary patriotic believers. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with zero preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than argument.

This is not a study that flatters one party and indicts the other. It catches the right and the left both. It asks the conservative whether he has married his country to God and refused to let anyone file for divorce, and it asks the progressive whether he fears religion in public only when it is the wrong religion. Most of all it implicates the leader and the writer. Bell does not stand outside this. He came up out of atheism into a faith already fused with the flag, he still has flags on his own platform he has not moved, and he writes from inside the indictment. So will you.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: Church and Empire: An 8-Week Study
guides.eyebrow: A pastoral, even-handed five-session study on how the church relates to political power, from a denarius in a trap to the end of Christendom, keeping the crucified King above every throne.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who feel the ground shifting under the faith in their country and want to know what is actually dying and what is not. It walks slowly through five essays by James Bell on the long marriage of church and empire, from the coin held up to trap Jesus, through the three centuries the church grew with no power at all, to the slow end of the arrangement that made Christianity the default religion of the West. It defines the hard words plainly, never sneers at the believer who grieves the change, and is built to be run by a busy volunteer with zero preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than argument.

This is not a study that flatters the people who want to seize the culture or the people who want to flee it. It catches both. It asks the Christian reaching for the levers of the state whether he has confused a borrowed majority with the work of the Spirit, and it asks the Christian who has washed his hands of public life whether he has called retreat by the name of holiness. Most of all it implicates the leader and the writer. Bell does not stand outside this. He has preached the render line as a permission slip, he has flags on his own platform he has not moved, he grieves the Sunday-closed store he grew up with, and he writes from inside the indictment. So will you.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: Consider the Birds
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on anxiety, and the peace Christ gives instead.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who are tired of being told to stop worrying by people who have never lain awake at three in the morning doing the math on a life that will not balance. It walks slowly through five movements drawn from James Bell's book Consider the Birds, on what anxiety is and is not, on the birds and the lilies Jesus told us to look at, on the peace Paul describes from a prison cell, on casting the weight onto the One who actually cares, and on the rest Christ offers to people who are tired in a way sleep does not touch. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with zero preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than advice.

This is not a study that tells anxious people their faith would fix them if it were stronger. It will not do that, and the leader must never let it. Some anxiety is the soul reaching for the wrong refuge, and the gospel speaks to that with power. Some anxiety is a body that has stopped producing what it needs, a wiring that misfires, a grief that has not finished, and that anxiety needs a doctor and is no more a sin than a broken arm. The study holds both without flinching, and refuses to make the second sound like the first. Most of all it implicates the leader and the writer. Bell does not stand outside this. He has lain awake. He has white-knuckled a morning he had no reason to fear and called it discernment. He has preached peace on a Sunday and gripped the wheel all the way home. He writes from inside the worry. So will you.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: Covenant
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on marriage as covenant — past the tips, into the cross.
guides.blurb:
This study is for married couples, engaged couples, and the small groups that carry them, who are tired of marriage taught as a list of techniques and want to know what the thing actually is. It walks slowly through five sessions on covenant against contract, on conflict and the long obedience of forgiveness, on headship and submission handled as mutual self-giving and never as a license to rule, on sex and faithfulness, on money and in-laws as the real pressure points where the vows get tested, and on the gospel shape of staying. It is built so a busy couple or a volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it. Every silence has a backup. Every session ends in prayer rather than in the argument the couple drove to group already having.

This is not a study that stands above marriage and dispenses advice. The writer is married, has five sons, and writes from inside the room where two people who love each other still wound each other on a Tuesday over nothing. He does not point from a safe distance. He has been the husband who kept a record he swore he had forgiven, who confused leading with getting his way, who let a screen become the easier thing to turn toward. He writes from inside the indictment. So will you. And the one place this study will not go, ever, is to tell anyone that the covenant is a command to endure being harmed. Where there is abuse there is no covenant to keep, only a person to protect and a sin to name, and the study says so plainly and points toward safety and help. The covenant images Christ laying his life down. It was never a permission for one spouse to take another's.
guides.audience: Married couples, engaged couples, and small groups

guides.title: Deep Roots
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on the doctrines we recite without using, the church we forgot we owe, and the single story Scripture has been telling all along.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals whose faith has outgrown the slogans it was handed and who suspect there is more under the floor than they have been shown. It walks slowly through five movements drawn from James Bell's book Deep Roots, on the gospel as news rather than advice and the God who turns out to be three, on whether a copied and contested Bible can still be trusted, on the fracture in the human heart and the costly grace and the God-man who answer it, on the councils and creeds and the Reformation that the church fought so we would not have to lose the gospel from scratch, and on the one story the whole library has been bending toward and the strange overlap of the ages we now live inside. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than a lecture.

This is not a study that flatters the people who already know the words. It will not let the lifelong churchgoer recite the creed as a museum piece, and it will not let the skeptic be dismissed as a fool for asking whether any of it happened. Bell takes the hardest form of every objection first, the village atheist and the wounded believer and the honest doubter, and grants what is true in each before he answers it, because a faith that cannot survive the strongest version of the question was never deep enough to stand on. Most of all the study implicates the writer and the leader. Bell does not teach this from a safe distance. He has preached the ladder and called it grace. He has prayed to a lonely idol while confessing the Trinity. He has used the Bible as a weapon and kept the ledger he claimed Christ had torn up. He writes from inside the room where people fall apart, and so will you.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: Economic Justice: An 8-Week Study
guides.eyebrow: A pastoral, even-handed five-session study that refuses both the preacher who blesses your portfolio and the politics that swallows the gospel, and keeps the cross at the center of money.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who are tired of money being preached as either a blessing to be claimed or a system to be torn down, and who want to know what Scripture actually says. It walks slowly through five essays by James Bell on what the Bible says about money, whether poverty is political, the economy God commanded in the Jubilee, the eye of the needle, and the difference between charity and justice. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with zero preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than argument.

This is not a study that flatters one party and indicts the other. It catches both tribes. It asks the Christian who has reduced justice to a check written on Tuesday whether he has built himself a hiding place, and it asks the Christian who has reduced the gospel to a voting bloc whether he still believes the cross can accomplish anything without a majority. Most of all it implicates the leader and the writer. Bell does not stand outside this. He has stretched toward security a thousand times and called it prudence, he holds notes and has expected return, he wears a shirt made by hands he will never meet. He writes from inside the indictment. So will you.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: Fatherhood in a Fatherless Age
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on the father wound, the father heart of God, and the long work of raising children who outlast you
guides.blurb:
This study is for the man who is trying to father well from a blueprint he was never handed. Maybe your own father was absent, or present and cold, or there and then gone. Maybe he was good and you still feel the weight of doing for your children what was done for you. We begin where most men begin, in the ache, and we move from the ache to the only Father whose love does not depend on your performance, and from there to the daily, unglamorous work of presence, discipline, blessing, and handing down a faith you have not finished learning yourself. It is written for fathers, for the men who will become them, and for the church that has too often handed men a job description instead of a gospel. No session asks you to pretend you have arrived. Every session assumes you are still in it.

The man writing this is not standing outside the subject explaining it. He was raised without a father. He came to God out of atheism, with no inherited faith and no felt picture of what a good father even was, and he is now raising five sons of his own, fathering forward into a gap he carried into adulthood. He has stood at a kitchen table and corrected a child in anger he regretted before the words were finished. He has traded presence for provision and called it love. He has waited, more than once, for a word of blessing from his own father that never came. He writes from inside the wound he is asking you to name, and the leader will lead from there too, because nothing in this study works from above. It only works shoulder to shoulder, one unfinished father next to another.
guides.audience: Fathers, fathers-to-be, men's groups, mentors, and any believer carrying a father wound
guides.sessionsLabel: 5 sessions (run as 5 weeks, a weekend retreat, or 10 shorter meetings)

guides.title: Grief and the God Who Wept
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on grief, loss, lament, and the hope that does not pretend the pain away.
guides.blurb:
This study is for the bereaved, for the small groups and grief groups that gather around them, and for the people who love someone in loss and do not know what to say. It walks slowly through five movements, on the God who stood at a friend's grave and wept before he opened it, on the permission to lament that the Psalms and Job and Lamentations hand back to a church that has forgotten how to cry out, on death named honestly as an enemy and not a friend, on a hope that refuses to deny the wound it is healing, and on the strange mercy by which the comfort we receive becomes comfort we can give. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than advice.

This is not a study that hurries the grieving toward closure, because closure is a word invented by people in a hurry, and grief is not a problem to be solved. It is love with nowhere to go, and it deserves better than a deadline. The study will not tell a mourner that everything happens for a reason, or that their person is in a better place, or that time heals, and the leader must never let the room do it either. It holds the hardest things without flinching. Death is real and it is wrong, the resurrection is real and it does not erase the grave's sting in the meantime, and a Christian may weep without shame and rage without losing faith. C. S. Lewis kept a journal in the weeks after his wife died and called it A Grief Observed, and he wrote things about God in it that no devotional would print. Nicholas Wolterstorff buried a son on a mountain and wrote Lament for a Son, refusing every comfort that made the death smaller. This study stands in that honest company. Most of all it implicates the leader and the writer. Bell does not stand outside this. He has stood at gravesides and said the right words and driven home undone. He has prayed for people whose prayers were not answered the way they begged. He writes from inside the loss. So will you.
guides.audience: The grieving, grief groups, and those who care for them

guides.title: How the Story Ends
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on the last things, holding open hands on the timeline and a closed fist on the center.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who are tired of being handed a chart and told it is the gospel. It is for the believer who has watched a date come and go, who has seen a church split over the rapture, who has read Revelation and felt more confused than comforted, and who suspects there is more here than a code to be cracked. It walks slowly through five movements on the end of the story, on how to read apocalyptic literature without turning it into a newspaper, on the three readings of the thousand years, on the rapture and the dispensational debate, on the already and the not yet that every serious Christian shares, and on the new creation that is the actual hope, the world made right rather than abandoned.

The editorial rule of this study is one thing, held without apology. Every major view of the end gets stated by its best advocate, in its strongest form, before anyone is allowed to argue against it. Premillennialism, postmillennialism, and amillennialism each get their best scholars and their strongest scriptural case. The dispensational rapture gets Darby and Scofield and Blaising at full strength before the alternatives answer. This is not a study that sells you one timeline as the answer and pretends the others are for the unserious. It refuses that, because faithful, careful, Bible-loving Christians have landed in all three camps for two thousand years, and a study that flattens them into one is lying to you about the church.

What the study will not compromise is the center, and the leader must guard it. Christ has come. Christ will come again. The dead will be raised. The world will be made right. On that, there is no open hand. The timeline is where the room is free to disagree. The creed is where it is not. And the writer stands inside all of it, because Bell came to faith from atheism arguing that the whole thing was a fairy tale for people afraid to die, and he has done his own date-math in the dark, and he has used the end times as an escape from a world he was supposed to love. He does not write from above this. He writes from inside it. So will you.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: Mishpat
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on God, the poor, and the justice the church forgot.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and anyone tired of hearing the word justice used as a flag for one political team and a curse word by the other, while the widow still waits at the gate and nobody in the room can say what the Bible actually means by the word. It walks slowly through five movements drawn from James Bell's book Mishpat, on the two Hebrew words the prophets refuse to separate, on the way God leans toward the poor and the foreigner on every page, on the worship God said He hated because of the worker underneath it, on the dividing wall the cross already tore down and the faces with no voice at the gate, and on the systemic sin that outlives the sinner and the shape love finally takes when it reaches the place where the powerless wait.

This is not a study that smuggles a party platform into the church under cover of a Bible word. It will not do that, and the leader must not let it. It is also not a study that lets the comfortable keep a private, spiritual gospel that never once disturbs a balance sheet or a pew. It refuses both, on purpose, all the way through. Most of all it implicates the leader and the writer. Bell does not stand above this. He has preached righteousness as if it meant only a soul scrubbed clean and never turned the room toward the gate. He has praised the Magnificat from a stage and gone home to a life arranged so he would never meet anyone Mary was singing about. He has used the basin to keep his own hands looking clean. He writes from inside the indictment. So will you.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: Questions Worth Asking
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study for skeptics and seekers asking, honestly, whether Christianity is true.
guides.blurb:
This study is for the person who does not believe, or is not sure, and is willing to look anyway. It is also for the friend who invited them, and who is about to learn how much harder it is to defend the faith than to assume it. The man who wrote it spent years as an atheist. He did not pray his way back. He read and argued and resisted his way back, slowly, over objections he still respects, and he has not forgotten what the other side of the door feels like. So nothing here is a trick. There is no emotional ambush waiting in session five, no moment where the lights dim and the music swells and you are asked to decide something you did not come to decide. Each session takes one hard question, states the strongest case against Christianity first and in full, and only then offers the response, and the response is allowed to be incomplete, because honest answers usually are.

This is not a study that wins arguments. It will not turn anyone into a debater, and the leader must not try. It walks through five questions in order. Whether there is anyone there at all. Whether science has buried God. Who Jesus actually was. Whether the resurrection happened. And what kind of step faith finally is, if the evidence does not force it. Along the way it names real thinkers by name, Lewis and Plantinga and Craig and Wright and Bauckham and Habermas, not as authorities to end the conversation but as people who have done the hard work and are worth reading. It is built to be run by a host who is not an expert, who may not know the answers and should say so when that is true. Every question carries the thinking behind it. Every objection is stated at full strength before it is answered. And no question, ever, is met with shame. A person who asks the hard thing out loud is doing the brave and honest thing, and the room exists to make that safe.
guides.audience: Skeptics, seekers, agnostics, and the friends who invited them

guides.title: Raising Believers
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on passing a durable faith to children in a secular age.
guides.blurb:
This study is for parents, grandparents, and small groups of families who want their children to know God and who are quietly terrified that wanting it is not enough. It walks slowly through five movements drawn from James Bell's book Raising Believers, on what the home is actually for in the formation of faith, on teaching the next generation the way the Shema commands, on answering the hard questions children ask instead of flinching from them, on a faith built to survive doubt and the years away from home, and on the parenting of grace rather than the parenting of fear. It is built to be run by a tired parent with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than a parenting tip.

This is not a study that promises a method that guarantees believing children. It will not do that, and the leader must never let it. Scripture is full of faithful parents whose children walked away, and the Bible itself records sons of godly men who wanted nothing to do with the God of their fathers. The home is the primary place where faith is handed on, and that is true and weighty and worth everything we have. But the home is not a machine that produces belief, and the gospel, not technique, is finally the hope of any child. The study holds both without flinching, and it refuses to sell parents a formula that will leave them crushed and self-blaming if a child wanders. Most of all it implicates the writer. Bell does not stand outside this. He has five sons. He has prayed over beds and not known if the prayers landed. He has answered a hard question badly and lain awake about it. He has parented from fear and called it diligence. He writes from inside the worry of a father who cannot save his own children and knows it. So will you.
guides.audience: Parents, grandparents, and small groups of families

guides.title: Teach Us to Pray
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on prayer, walking slowly through the words Jesus gave us.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who have been praying for years and quietly suspect they have never learned how, and for those who have stopped praying because the words ran out or the heavens went silent. It walks through the prayer Jesus taught when his own followers, who had watched him pray, asked him to teach them. Not a book on prayer. A school of prayer, run on the words of the Lord's Prayer itself, one clause at a time. Who we pray to and dare to call Father. What we are really asking when we ask for his name to be honored and his kingdom to come. The daily bread that ends our pretending we feed ourselves. The forgiveness we receive and the forgiveness we are bound to extend. And the prayer prayed in the dark, when the asking goes unanswered and the only faithful thing left is to keep asking anyway.

This is not a study that will hand anyone a technique for getting God to perform. It will refuse that, and the leader must refuse it too. Prayer is not a lever. It is a child speaking to a Father, and some in the room have no working picture of a father at all, because theirs left, or never came, or stayed and wounded. Bell knows that pew. He was raised without a father. He came to God out of atheism, with no inherited faith to lean on and every reason to doubt the word Father meant anything. He is not standing outside this study explaining prayer to people who struggle with it. He is one of them. He has prayed into a ceiling. He has gone months saying the right words to a God who felt absent. He writes from inside the silence, and the leader will lead from there too.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: The Captive Church
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on nationalism, empire, and the cost of a free church.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who are tired of watching the church reach for the kingdoms of this world on the terms the world offers and then call the reach faithfulness. It walks slowly through five movements drawn from James Bell's book The Captive Church, beginning on the mountain where Jesus was offered every kingdom for one bent knee and refused, moving through the naming of Christian nationalism on the left and the right, the long marriage of the church and the empire that began under Constantine, the question of what bears the image of God when they brought him a coin to trap him, the water of cultural captivity we cannot feel because we were born in it, and the cost of a church free enough to say that Jesus is Lord and Caesar is not. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with zero preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than a partisan verdict.

This is not a study about politics, and the leader must say so out loud, again and again, because every person who walks in will assume it is. It is a study about the cross, and about who the church belongs to. It will not tell anyone which way to vote, and it will not let either tribe sit comfortable while the other gets named. It indicts every side by the same cross, because the prophet who indicts only the other tribe is not a prophet but a partisan with a Bible. Most of all it implicates the writer and the leader. Bell does not stand on the shore pointing at the swimmers. He came to faith out of atheism into a Christianity already fused with a flag. He grew up inside the fusion. He has wanted the mountain. He has run the double standard, excused his own side, baptized his own politics, and kept high places he swore were not high places. He writes from inside the captivity, toward a freedom he has not arrived at. So will you.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: The Country We Have Not Seen
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on heaven, hell, and the life to come, and the hope that produces courage instead of escape.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who have grown tired of a hope that sounds like clouds and harps and have begun to suspect that the Bible promises something larger, stranger, and far more solid. It walks slowly through five movements on the last things. It clears away the wrong picture of heaven and recovers the biblical hope. It follows N.T. Wright into the resurrection of the body and the redemption of the new earth, what he calls life after life-after-death. It faces hell honestly, laying the historic view of eternal conscious punishment, the conditionalist view, and the reach of universalism each at full strength, without flinching and without gloating. It sits with the intermediate state and the communion of saints, holding grief and hope together at the graveside. And it ends where the whole faith ends, with how the morning that is coming shapes the long defeat we are living now. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than advice.

This is not a study that hands frightened people easy certainties or uses hell as a whip. It will not do that, and the leader must never let it. James Bell came to faith out of atheism, and the doctrine of hell was the thing he held hardest against God, so he does not pretend it is comfortable now. He takes the objection at full weight because he once made it himself. And he does not stand outside any of this. He was raised without a father and has buried people he loved, and he has felt the particular ache of grieving a presence he barely had. He has wanted to flee a world that breaks his heart, and he has wanted to give up the horizon and call it wisdom. He writes from inside the longing and the doubt and the grief. So will you.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: The Distracted Soul: Attention, Technology, and the Life You Actually Have
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on attention, the phone, and the slow recovery of a present life with God and the people in front of you.
guides.blurb:
This study is for anyone who has felt the quiet ache of a day spent on the phone and not in their life, who picks the device up to check one thing and surfaces an hour later having checked nothing that mattered, who can no longer sit in a silent room without reaching for it, who has read to a child while glancing at a screen and felt the small betrayal of it. It is for the Christian who cannot pray for five minutes without the urge to scroll, for the pastor watching a congregation grow more anxious and less present year by year, and for the skeptic who suspects, rightly, that something is being done to all of us and is not sure the church has anything to say about it.

This is not a study that will hand anyone a productivity system or a digital cleanse with a finish line. It will refuse that, and the leader must refuse it too. Attention is not a resource to be optimized. It is the substance of a life and the form love takes, and a soul that cannot attend cannot love God or anyone else, however much it wants to. The session moves through five movements: the stolen hour and what the feed is quietly making us into; the research on the phone-based childhood, taken at its strongest and tested against Scripture; the practice of presence in Sabbath, silence, and the desert tradition; the slow word of Scripture set against the scroll and the renewing of the mind; and a reordering of the household and the phone that is a way of life, not a tip list.

Bell does not write this from a mountain above the problem. He writes it with his own phone face-down on the desk, having lost his own hours to it, having looked up from it at one of his five sons and seen the boy waiting. He is not the man who beat the machine and is now reporting back. He is inside the indictment with everyone in the room. He will say so, and the leader must too, because a study on attention led by someone pretending to have mastered theirs would be its own kind of lie.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: The First Steps
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study for the brand new Christian, on what just happened and how to walk the long road that follows.
guides.blurb:
This study is for the person to whom something real has just happened, for the recently baptized still dripping and unsure what comes next, and for the seeker standing at the edge of it all, wondering what they would be signing up for. It walks slowly through five movements. What the new birth actually is and how a person can know it took. The Bible, what it is and how to read it without drowning on page one. Prayer, which is nothing more complicated than honest speech toward a Father who already knows. The church, the people you cannot follow Jesus without. And the long road, repentance and obedience and the slow reordering of an ordinary life over years. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every old church word gets defined on the spot rather than assumed.

This is not a study that hands a new believer a list of rules and tells them to perform. It will not do that, and the leader must never let it. The thing that happened to these people happened by grace, which is the old word for love they did not earn and cannot pay back, and everything that follows runs on the same grace or it does not run at all. The study refuses two opposite errors. It refuses the cheap welcome that asks nothing and pretends following Jesus costs nothing, because it costs everything. And it refuses the heavy yoke that buries a new Christian under expectations before they have learned to stand, because that is how you crush a seedling. Most of all it implicates the writer. Bell came to faith from atheism. He knows what it is to stand outside the whole thing certain it was a fairy tale, and he knows the strange morning he woke up unable to deny it any longer. He did not grow up in this. He arrived as a stranger and had to learn the first steps himself, badly, with no one to teach him. He writes from inside the beginning, not above it. So will you.
guides.audience: New believers, the recently baptized, and seekers

guides.title: The Forgotten God
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on the Holy Spirit, the personal presence of God who gives life.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who have spent years in church and somehow ended up with two persons of the Trinity they could describe and a third they could not. The Father they picture. The Son they love. The Spirit has been left a kind of holy vapor, a power source, an influence, the part of God you mention at the end of a prayer and then forget. This is not a small mistake. It is the loss of God himself, present, personal, indwelling, the very breath by which the dead are made alive. The study walks slowly through five movements. Who the Spirit is and why the church treats him as an afterthought. The new birth, regeneration, the Spirit who raises the spiritually dead, including the writer, who was an atheist until the Spirit did the one thing argument never could. The slow work of the fruit and the difference between being changed and merely performing. The contested question of the gifts, where continuationist and cessationist are both given their strongest case and the group is held together across the divide. And the Spirit in our weakness, the One who prays in us when we have no words, the down payment of a world being made new.

This is not a study that will pick the group's side in the old fights over tongues and prophecy and healing. It will not do that, and the leader must never let it. The continuationist case will be put at full strength and so will the cessationist, and the aim is a room that can disagree about gifts while worshiping the same Spirit. Most of all the study implicates the leader and the writer. Bell does not stand outside this. He spent years certain there was no God and no soul and no Spirit, and the thing that finally undid him was not a better argument. It was a presence he had no category for. He writes from inside the new birth he did not author and cannot explain. So will you.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: The Hardest Word
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on forgiveness, what it costs, and the freedom on the far side of it.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who have been told to forgive by people who have never been hurt the way they have been hurt. It walks slowly through five movements on what forgiveness is and is not, on the debt we could never repay and the servant who would not forgive a fraction of what he had been forgiven, on releasing a person who never said sorry and never will, on the false choice between mercy and accountability, and on the slow obedience of forgiving when the wound does not close and the one you most need to forgive is God or yourself. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with zero preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than advice.

This is not a study that tells wounded people their pain would lift if they just let it go. It will not do that, and the leader must never let it. Forgiveness is not forgetting, not excusing, not pretending the wrong was smaller than it was. It is the costly decision to release a debt that is real, to absorb a loss that someone else caused and will not repay. Miroslav Volf wrote Exclusion and Embrace from inside the wreckage of the Balkans, and he would not let forgiveness become amnesia, because to forget the wrong is to side with the wrongdoer against the victim. The study holds the cost and the freedom together and refuses to make either cheap. Most of all it implicates the leader and the writer. Bell does not stand outside this. He grew up without a father, and he has spent years learning what it is to forgive a man who never asked to be forgiven and never came back to ask. He has held a grudge and called it standing for justice. He writes from inside the unforgiveness. So will you.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: The Health of the Pastor: A Study for Leaders and Those Who Love Them
guides.eyebrow: A warm, plainspoken five-session study on the exhaustion, hiddenness, and quiet despair of the people who shepherd us, built for boards and leadership teams to read alongside the pastor they are trying to keep.
guides.blurb:
This study is for elder boards, deacon teams, leadership councils, and the spouses and friends who love a pastor and can see that he is tired in a way that worries them. It walks slowly through five essays by James Bell on why pastors leave, why so many of them are quietly depressed, how a man loses his soul while building a church, why his hidden life is the first thing to starve, and why a church should require its pastor to rest. It is built to be led by a busy volunteer with zero preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than a plan.

This is not a study that scolds the pastor for being weak or scolds the board for being blind. It does something harder. It asks the leadership to look honestly at a structure they helped build, one that can consume the most faithful man in the room and then mourn him at the graveside in genuine confusion about what went wrong. Bell does not stand outside this. He nearly left the ministry himself. He has preached resurrection on a Sunday he could not feel his own pulse by Wednesday. He writes from inside the broom tree, not from a safe distance, and he asks you to read this with your own pastor in the room, or at least with his face in your mind.

A plain word before you begin. This material touches burnout, and in two sessions it touches clinical depression directly. Depression is not a failure of faith, and exhaustion is not a character flaw. Where a pastor is struggling with depression or any mental illness, the right and faithful step is a medical doctor and a licensed counselor, the same as for any other illness of the body. If a pastor is in crisis, call or text 988. Seeking help is an act of faith, not a confession of failure. There is no shame anywhere in this room.
guides.audience: Pastors, elder boards, and church leadership teams

guides.title: The Prayers We Were Never Taught
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on suffering and lament, anchored in the Psalms and Job.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who have sat in a church that knew how to praise and did not know what to do with a person who could not. It walks slowly through five movements on suffering and the lost prayer the church forgot how to pray. It begins with lament as a vanished form, the cost of a worship that only ascends and never cries out. It moves into the lament psalms themselves, the how long of Psalm 13 and the unbroken dark of Psalm 88, the one prayer in the book that does not resolve. It sits with Job and the friends who explained too much, the failure of the tidy answer, the long silence in the ash. It comes to the cross, where God does not stand above the sufferer offering an explanation but climbs down inside the suffering and cries the lament himself. And it ends not in resolution but in a hope that refuses to be denial, the difference between an answer and a presence, between the question closed and the question carried.

This is not a study that will hurry anyone out of their grief. It will not hand a suffering person the platitude that everything happens for a reason, and the leader must never let it. Walter Brueggemann taught the church the cost of what he called the loss of lament, the price a community pays when it permits only praise. The Psalms gave Israel a language for the dark that the modern church has largely thrown away, and Job stands as the long protest God did not rebuke. The study holds the honesty of Psalm 88 without flinching. That psalm ends in darkness, and that is allowed. Most of all it implicates the leader and the writer. James Bell does not stand outside this. He was raised without a father, and he came to God out of atheism, and he has prayed prayers that got no answer he could see. He has stood at gravesides and had nothing to say that did not sound like a lie. He writes from inside the loss. So will you.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: The Rest We Refuse
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on Sabbath, rest, and the God who stopped on the seventh day.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who are tired in a way that sleep does not touch, who suspect their exhaustion is not only a scheduling problem but a soul problem, and who have a vague guilt about rest they cannot quite name. It walks slowly through five movements on the Sabbath, on the God who rested when he did not have to, on rest as a refusal to be defined by what we produce, on the Lord who said the Sabbath was made for man and not man for the Sabbath, on what a day of actual rest looks like when you stop dressing your restlessness in spiritual language, and on the rest that still remains for the people of God. It leans on Walter Brueggemann's Sabbath as Resistance, on Abraham Joshua Heschel's The Sabbath, on Eugene Peterson, on Tim Keller, and on Dietrich Bonhoeffer, and it tries to earn every one of them rather than name-drop them. It is built so a busy volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than advice.

This is not a study that will hand you a tidy schedule and call it holiness. It refuses the productivity sermon dressed as discipleship, the version of Sabbath that becomes one more thing to perform well. And it refuses the opposite error too, the spiritualized excuse that says rest is for the weak and the serious Christian grinds. Both are lies, and the leader must not let either win the room. Most of all it implicates the writer. Bell is terrible at this. He is a pastor whose one day off bleeds into hospital visits and half-answered emails, who has preached on rest with a phone buzzing in his pocket, who has called his inability to stop a calling. He came to faith from atheism, where work was the only god on offer and you were what you made. He was raised without a father, which taught him early that the weight was his alone to carry and no one was coming to lift it. He has five sons who needed a father who could stop, and a God who keeps inviting him to a rest he keeps declining. He writes from inside the refusal. So will you.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: The Self You Were Sold: Identity in a Self-Made Age
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on who you are, walking out of the project of self-creation and into an identity that was given before it was ever performed.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and anyone exhausted by the work of being themselves. Not the work of a hard job or a hard week. The work of holding up a self you have to keep building, defending, updating, and selling, with no day off and no final version. It is for the person who has done everything the age told them to do, who has looked inward and found their truest self and become it and posted it, and who still lies awake suspecting that none of it is holding. And it is for the skeptic who has heard the church offer a thin answer to the deepest question a human being asks, who am I, and walked away unconvinced, and who deserves a better account than the one they were given.

The age we live in handed everyone a single instruction and called it freedom. Look inward. Find your true self. Define yourself, on your own terms, against every inherited expectation, and then become that self and present it to the world for approval. It sounds like liberation. For many it has become a sentence to hard labor, the labor of being your own author and your own audience at once, manufacturing a self from nothing and then anxiously watching to see whether it sells. This study walks slowly through how that self was invented, why it is so tiring, and what the older answer was before the modern one replaced it. Identity not as an achievement you assemble but as a gift you receive. Not the self you make, but the self you are given.

Bell does not write this from above. He came to faith from atheism, which means he spent years building a self with no God in the picture, looking inward for a foundation and finding sand. He was raised without a father, which means the question of who he was had a hole in the middle of it where an inherited name should have been. He has performed a self he was not sure was real. He has measured his worth by the room's reaction and gone home empty. He writes from inside the exhaustion, not at a clean distance from it, and the leader will lead from there too.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: The Undivided Life
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on following Jesus through an ordinary week.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and individuals who were handed a faith for Sundays and a calendar for the other six days, and who have lived in the gap between them so long they mistook the gap for adulthood. It walks slowly through five movements drawn from James Bell's book The Undivided Life, on the life lived in boxes and the one life offered whole, on marriage as covenant and the home that forms us, on the refusal to rest and the limits of the body, on all honest work as a calling, and on the rival god of money and the wholeness that is the real standard of a life. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than advice.

This is not a study about doing more. It is a study about being one person. The divided man is exhausted in a way he cannot explain to his doctor, because he is running several incompatible lives on the same set of bones, preaching generosity and hoarding, counseling patience and raging in traffic, believing God holds the future and lying awake managing it. The gospel offers, before it offers anything else, the rejoining of the man, one life surrendered to one Lord who is finally allowed to walk down the hallway and turn on the lights in the rooms we kept dark. And it implicates the leader and the writer first. Bell does not stand outside this. He came to faith from atheism and arrived with the convert's certainty that everything had changed, then discovered over slow years he had let almost nothing change in the places no one could see. He has lived in the boxes. He runs hot, confuses output with worth, has refused rest and called it devotion, has served the rival god and built a fortress called security. He writes from inside the dividing. So will you.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: The Work of Our Hands
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on work and vocation, and the faith that has to survive Monday.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and anyone who has sat in a pew on Sunday feeling that their faith was real and large, and then walked into a job on Monday where it seemed to shrink to nothing. It is for the believer who suspects, somewhere underneath, that the real work of God happens on a stage with a microphone and that their own forty hours at a desk or a register or a job site are spiritually beside the point. It walks slowly through five movements on what work is and was meant to be, on Eden where God himself worked and called it good, on the thorns and the sweat that came after, on the lie that splits the world into sacred jobs and secular ones, on the idol that work becomes when it stops being what we do and starts being who we are, and on the strange promise that our labor is not finally lost. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than advice.

This is not a study that will tell you to find your passion and the rest will take care of itself, because most work is not passion and most weeks are not inspired, and the gospel has something to say to the ordinary Tuesday and not only to the calling that thrills you. It refuses two lies at once. The first says ordinary work does not matter to God, that only ministry counts, and the study takes that lie apart with Luther and Dorothy Sayers and the whole doctrine of vocation. The second says work is everything, the place we earn our worth and prove we exist, and the study names that as the idol it is. Most of all the study implicates the writer. Bell does not stand outside this. He is a pastor, and the pastorate is a job, a job he has loved into an idol, a job he has hidden behind, a job whose busyness he has called faithfulness when it was really fear. He has made the work of God a way of avoiding God. He writes from inside the problem. So will you.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: When Faith Has Questions
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on doubt, deconstruction, and the God who is not afraid of either.
guides.blurb:
This study is for the believer whose faith has started asking questions the church taught him not to ask, for the small group that wants to talk about doubt without anyone reaching for the panic button, and for the skeptic who came along to be honest rather than to be fixed. It walks slowly through the hardest questions faith faces, the suffering that does not resolve, the God who hides, the Scripture whose reliability is contested, the hypocrisy that did real damage, the doctrine of hell, and the apparent quarrel with science. It refuses to win cheaply. Every hard question gets stated at its strongest before anyone answers it, because a faith that has to misquote the objection to survive it was never worth keeping.

This is not a study that shames the doubter or flatters him. The man who wrote it came to faith from atheism and was raised without a father, and he remembers the inside of the question, not just the answer to it. So the study draws a careful line, fairly and without contempt for either side. There is honest doubt that is faith asking God a hard question while refusing to let go of his sleeve, the doubt of the father who cried I believe, help my unbelief, and there is deconstruction that has already decided to leave and is only narrating the exit. The study respects both more than they expect. It will not pretend the leaver has no reasons, and it will not pretend the doubter is in danger of hell for doubting. It ends where Job ended and where Thomas ended, with a faith that has been through the fire, not a faith that never asked.
guides.audience: Skeptics, Christians with questions, small groups, and individuals

guides.title: When It All Comes Apart
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on faith deconstruction, handled pastorally, for the person taking an inherited faith apart to see what is actually true.
guides.blurb:
This study is for the person pulling a faith apart piece by piece, for the friends and pastors who love them and do not know what to say, and for small groups willing to sit with hard questions without panicking. It walks slowly through five movements, on what you are actually taking apart when you say you are deconstructing, on whether doubt is a sin and the Bible's long line of honest doubters, on the wounds that come when the church itself is the reason, on rebuilding on rock rather than on the rubble of what you tore down, and on a faith small enough to be true and strong enough to hold weight. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than a verdict.

This is not a study that tries to talk anyone out of their questions, and the leader must never let it become that. Deconstruction is not a betrayal and it is not a fad. It is what an honest person does when the answers they were handed stop carrying weight. Many people taking their faith apart are not leaving Jesus. They are leaving a version of him somebody sold them, and the difference between those two departures is the whole question this study exists to help people see. Some of what gets torn down deserves to come down, the cultural baggage, the borrowed certainty, the politics dressed as the gospel. Some of what gets torn down is the load-bearing wall, and the cost of pulling it out only shows up later. The study holds both without flinching, and it refuses to make faithful sifting sound like abandonment or to make abandonment sound like courage. Most of all it implicates the writer and the leader. Bell does not stand outside this. He is a pastor, and pastors like him did the bundling, wrapping God and the institution and the politics into one package and handing it over as though it were all the same thing. He has watched people leave over what the church did and called it their unbelief. He has the questions too. So will you.
guides.audience: Those deconstructing, their friends and pastors, and small groups

guides.title: Where Is God When It Hurts: Suffering and the Goodness of God
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on the problem of evil, the providence of God, and the hope that does not disappoint.
guides.blurb:
This study is for the person who has stood at a hospital bed, or a graveside, or in the wreckage of a marriage or a diagnosis, and asked the oldest question there is. If God is good, and God is able, why this. It is for the skeptic who left the faith over a child's cancer ward and was never given an answer worth the name, and for the Christian still inside the faith carrying a question the church kept handing them platitudes for. It is for the pastor who has run out of things to say at funerals. It does not promise to solve the problem of evil, because no honest book ever has, and the ones that pretend to are the ones that wound. It promises something harder and more durable. It takes the objection at its full and terrible strength, refuses every cheap answer, and walks toward the only response Scripture finally gives, which is not an argument but a Person who entered the suffering himself.

The five sessions move in order. First the question stated without flinching, the way the honest atheist states it, so well that the believer in the room feels it too. Then the doctrine of providence held without tidy resolution, a God who permits what he hates and works it toward an end we cannot see from inside it. Then the book of Job, where God answers the sufferer not with an explanation but with a whirlwind and a thousand questions, and rebukes the friends who had the formula. Then the cross, where the God who permits suffering does not stay outside it but enters it, bleeds inside it, dies inside it. And finally the hope that does not explain suffering away but defeats it, the resurrection and the new creation where every tear is wiped from every face. Bell does not write this from a safe distance. He came to God from atheism, and the problem of evil was the wall he could not get over for years. He has buried people he loved and prayed for healing that did not come. He is not solving a puzzle for you. He is standing in the rubble with you, pointing at the only light he has found that the dark could not put out.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: Where Your Treasure Is
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on money, the heart, and the freedom Christ offers.
guides.blurb:
This is the small-group companion to James Bell's book Where Your Treasure Is, and it is not about the economy. It is about your heart and what it has quietly done with money. It walks slowly through five sessions on the heart that follows its treasure, the contentment we keep mistaking for resignation, the rich fool who confused a full barn with a safe soul, the anxiety that drives our reaching, and the strange freedom of the open hand. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than argument.

This is not a study that flatters the generous and indicts the greedy, because Bell does not believe the line runs there. It catches the man who gives and still grips, the woman who has little and still worships what she lacks, the giver who has used his giving to stop the question before it reached his heart. Most of all it implicates the writer. Bell does not stand outside this. He has lain awake doing arithmetic he called prudence. He has felt his chest loosen at a number in an account and called the loosening peace. He has loved his five sons and let the love become a reason to reach for more and never enough. He writes from inside the indictment about money, not above it. So will you. The question is never whether you may have money. The question is what your heart has done with it, and whether you can hear, under all the wanting, the voice of the One who became poor so that you could be free.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

guides.title: Why We Still Need Each Other
guides.eyebrow: A five-session study on the church, the body of Christ, and the call to belong to a people who will let you down.
guides.blurb:
This study is for small groups, adult Sunday school classes, and anyone who has loved the church and been wounded by it in roughly equal measure, which is to say almost everyone who has stayed long enough to know what they are talking about. It walks slowly through five movements on what the church actually is, on the life together that Bonhoeffer described from inside a community that the state would soon scatter and kill, on the marks and the mess of a church that is a hospital of sinners and not a museum of saints, on the church sent into a culture that no longer assumes the faith, and on the hard grace of committing to a flawed people instead of leaving the moment they prove flawed. It is built to be run by a busy volunteer with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it, every silence has a backup, and every session ends in prayer rather than a tidy resolution.

This is not a study that defends the church by pretending it is fine. It will not do that, and the leader must never let it. The church has covered up abuse, baptized politics, traded its prophets for its donors, and bored a watching world half to death. The study takes all of that seriously and refuses to flinch. But it also refuses the easy exit, the conviction common to the wounded that the answer to a hypocritical church is no church, that a Christian can follow Jesus alone with a podcast and a Bible app. The New Testament knows no such Christian. Bell writes as a working pastor who has watched the church fail up close, who has been the failure more than once, and who loves her anyway, the way you love a family you cannot disown because it is the only family there is. He does not stand outside this. He has been the hypocrite in the pulpit. He writes from inside the body. So will you.
guides.audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals
